 Early voting totals are way up in St. Louis County
 But it’s not clear if more people plan to vote—or if more people are simply opting for early voting. 
 by 
 Sarah Fenske & Ryan Krull 
 October 27, 2026 at 5:45 AM 
 October 26, 2026 
 Photography by mrolands / iStock / Getty Images Plus 
 Early voting is now underway across Missouri. 
 One week into early voting in St Louis County, more people have already cast a ballot than in all of early voting four years ago, during the last midterm election. “Turnout has been strong,” says Eric Fey, the Democratic director of elections for St. Louis County. “We just don’t know what that means yet.”
 In 2022, the county had seven locations where 56,000 voters cast a ballot ahead in the two weeks before election day. Since early voting opened last week Tuesday, over 60,000 ballots have been cast at the county’s 21 early voting locations.

 However, Fey says that we don’t yet know if this means that the midterms in the county will have high turnout, or if the county will just see fewer people cast a ballot on election day. 
 The county provides a tracker of where early votes are being cast. It shows West County and mid-South County putting up big numbers, specifically the Daniel Boone and Grant’s View libraries. But since anyone in the county can vote anywhere, that doesn’t necessarily mean those are neighborhoods with high turnout—only that people found it convenient to cast ballots there.
 In the city, as of Saturday afternoon, nearly 9,500 voters had cast early ballots. Ben Borgmeyer, the Democratic director of elections for the city, called the number solid but not remarkable. Unlike St. Louis County, the city does not have a contentious congressional election on the ballot this November (because Democrats dominate the district encompassing the city, U.S. Rep. Wesley Bell’s tougher challenge was in the primary). Nor is the mayor on the ballot this year, as is the case for the county executive.
 As usual, the most popular early voting location is the Buder library in St. Louis Hills. Twice as many people have voted there compared to the next most popular early voting location.
 In St. Louis County, high turnout could suggest wide interest in the 2nd congressional district race, which pits 13-year incumbent Ann Wagner (R-Ballwin) against military veteran Fred Wellman, a Democrat seeking to ride an anticipated blue wave on November 3. Wellman has produced several polls suggesting he’s running neck and neck with Wagner, something no challenger has been able to do on election day. (Wagner’s closest Democratic challenger, Cort VanOstran, won 47 percent of the vote in 2018 to Wagner’s 51 percent.) 
 High turnout—if that is indeed what St. Louis County is seeing—could also be a boon to efforts to stop Amendment 3, which seeks to again ban abortion, two years after voters enshrined it as a right in Missouri’s constitution. In 2024, 67 percent of St. Louis County voters cast ballots in favor of abortion rights, and running up a high margin in the state’s most populous county will be critical for Amendment 3 this year, as the race is expected to be tight.
 High turnout in the city could also help stop Amendment 3. The city voted 82 percent in favor of abortion rights in 2024, by far the largest margin in the state. 
 Among other high-profile matters, voters are also being asked to weigh in on Amendment 6, which would make it harder for the legislature to overturn the will of voters, and Proposition A, which would put in place the Trump-backed congressional maps passed by the legislature in 2025. Signs all over St. Louis city and county urge voters to “vote yes on 6, the rest are tricks”—with the hope that high margins in the St. Louis area can outweigh the desires of more rural, Republican-leaning voters.
 Ryan Krull 
 Ryan Krull is a staff writer for St. Louis Magazine.
